uncited: This family addresses the computational cost and visual fidelity trade-off in isosurface extraction by varying the resolution of the output mesh based on geometric complexity and view importance.
Unlike fixed-resolution methods, these techniques dynamically adjust the level of detail (LOD) to maintain interactive frame rates while preserving critical surface features [S1].

The core distinction lies in how they manage the boundary between different resolution levels: some methods avoid reconnection entirely to maximize speed, while others use explicit patching or oracle-driven traversal to ensure watertightness.

All methods in this family operate on a discretized domain, typically a regular grid (Cartesian, octree, or tetrahedral) where each cell contains scalar values or occupancy states at its vertices or centers.
**Surface Determination**: A criterion is applied to identify surface locations.
In isosurface methods, this involves comparing scalar values against a threshold (isovalue) to detect sign changes or equality [30-isosurface-extraction.md].
In blocky meshing, this involves checking occupancy states or material IDs to identify exposed boundaries [31-blocky-meshing.md].
**Mesh Coherence**: Adjacent primitives are merged or connected to form a coherent mesh, often requiring vertex merging to avoid duplicates and ensure watertightness [30-isosurface-extraction.md].
The need for multiresolution extraction arises from the high computational cost of extracting detailed isosurfaces from large volumetric datasets in real-time.
Early approaches often used fixed grids, leading to either excessive detail in flat regions or insufficient detail in complex areas.
The development of adaptive methods, particularly those utilizing octrees and view-dependent criteria, allowed for efficient rendering of complex surfaces.

The specific techniques described here, including the use of oracles and projected size adjustments, were developed to address the specific challenges of interactive sculpting and visualization, where frame rate stability and visual continuity are paramount [S1].
